title: The first mountain, from the top
hook: you've been climbing for 329 days: today, turn around and look down the trail

segments.voice: Last week, five houses heard in their own words, then two questions at your own door: a thread on the wrist, and what to do when someone isn't kind. Your line was your worth isn't up for a vote. Day three hundred thirty.
screen: `YOUR WORTH ISN'T UP FOR A VOTE.`

segments.voice: Near the top of a long climb, there's a moment. You've been staring at your feet for hours: the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Your legs hurt. You haven't looked up in a long time. And then the trail flattens, and there's nowhere higher to step, and you turn around. And the whole path is lying there below you, the parking lot tiny, the first bend you thought was steep looking like nothing at all. You did that. One step a day. Today there's no new idea. Today we turn around.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET FOR MONTHS.` → `THE TRAIL FLATTENS.` → `TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Look down the trail. At the very bottom, camp one: twenty-one words. Namaste, om, dharma, shanti, karma, atman, Brahman, seva, bhakti, moksha, and the others. Some you may have said for years without knowing what they meant; some were new. Either way, they were Sanskrit. A little higher, camp two: the stories. Ganesha and his broken tusk. Hanuman's leap. The whole Ramayana as a serial, Rama and Sita and the long road home. Then the Mahabharata's cliffhangers, leaving two armies on a field. Higher still, camp three: the practices. Breath, mantra, a small shrine, a flame at sunset, food as offering, the temple, the festivals. The path stopped being something you listened to and became something you did. Then the steep part, camp four: the Bhagavad Gita, all eighteen chapters, about seven hundred verses, read in order. Arjuna dropping his bow. Krishna's answer. Chapter eleven's terrifying vision. And at the end, the line where Krishna hands the choice back to Arjuna: do as you choose. You read the whole thing. And the last stretch, camp five: the depths. The Upanishads, Isha, Kena, Katha, Mandukya. The three paths of action, devotion and knowledge. Advaita and Dvaita side by side, never ranked. The Yoga Sutras' first line: now, yoga. A track of your own choosing. And last week, a guest in six other houses. That's the first mountain. Not the whole range; the first mountain. A traditional teacher might say you haven't finished anything. You've just learned to walk. But from up here, the steps add up.
screen: `CAMP ONE: TWENTY-ONE WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: THE WHOLE GITA.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: The whole year in one sit. Close your eyes. Breathe in, and remember a word from camp one, any word. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember a story: a monkey, a bridge, a chariot. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember something you did: a flame, a mantra, a meal. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember one line from the Gita that stayed. Breathe out. Breathe in, and remember one question from the depths: who am I? Then just rest at the top. The bell holds the time.
Shikhara, a mountain peak. Twenty-one words, the stories, the practices, the whole Gita and the depths, held for two minutes at once, the way a view holds a trail.
Your line: look how far. Today, tell one person one thing you know now that you didn't know a year ago. Just one. Day three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the end of a period of study or a vow with a pause to look back, often with a puja or a visit to a teacher to give thanks; people who finish reading the whole Gita sometimes celebrate its completion.

match.prompt: each camp and what it held — tap the pairs.

myth: the Bhagavad Gita has eighteen chapters
all eighteen, about seven hundred verses, read in order in camp four.
reaching the top of year one means the path is finished
it's the first mountain, not the whole range: from here, the ranges begin.
this year taught Advaita as the right answer and Dvaita as the wrong one
they were taught side by side as electives, never ranked.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of a long climb. what's the first thing to do?
options: start up the next peak immediately.
turn around and look how far you came.
check how many steps other people took.
fork.reveal: today is for turning around. no new idea: just the view, and the steps adding up.

original.note: Sanskrit śikhara: a mountain peak, and also the name for the tall tower over a north Indian temple's shrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: the summit is the end of the climb.
what it means: the top of the first mountain: a place to turn around and see the whole trail at once.
what a scholar hears: the shikhara, peak, over a north Indian temple's inner shrine is built to echo a mountain, often read as Meru or Kailash.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.1 (now, the teaching of yoga)

notes: Summit recap of year one, drawn from the outline's camp and week headings (camp 1 words, Ganesha, Hanuman, Ramayana serial, Mahabharata cliffhangers, practices, the Gita, Upanishads, three paths, Advaita/Dvaita, Yoga Sutras, lineage track, neighbor visits). If camps 2–3 were written differently, the recap should be adjusted.
'About seven hundred verses' is the conventional count of the Gita (700 in the common recension).
Shikhara as echoing Meru/Kailash: a common art-historical reading; confirm.
The 'do as you choose' line is 18.63 in most numberings (the outline puts day 224 at 18.59–18.66).

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens with the sweeping 'anyone who has climbed a real hill knows'; the teach no longer tells the listener what they had said or learned; 'the Hindu tradition would say' (speaking for a whole tradition) softened to 'a traditional teacher might say'.
